To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

finding a vertex of a prescribed outdegree in a tournament Tn requires Θ(k(n) lgαn) probes, where α is any fixed constant and k(n)=Θ(n), and finding a vertex of indegree Θ(n) or outdegree Θ(n2) in T requires Θ(n2) edge probes.
finding a vertex of a given outdegree k(n-1)/2 in Tn takes Θ(n^k) time, while finding a vertex of the maximum outdegree in a tournament takes Ω(n^2) time.

the complexity of the following problems are Θ(nk): (1) finding a vertex with prescribed outdegree, and (2) finding a vertex of minimum indegree, and (3) finding a vertex which is not a source, and (4) finding a vertex whose outdegree exceeds its indegree.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: 1) What is the complexity of finding certain trees in tournaments? 2) What are the differences between finding certain trees in general tournaments and transitive tournaments? 3) What are the relationships between these problems and the problems of finding certain trees on general and transitive digraphs?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the complexity of the selection problems in Tn is O(n lgα n), Θ(nk), Θ(n2), or Θ(n3) depending on the parameters k, n, and α.
the complexity of selecting a vertex of prescribed degree is linear in transitive tournaments, but super-linear in non-transitive tournaments.

, in general tournaments, the complexity of finding directed paths, cycles, or vertices of prescribed degree is Θ(n lgαn) where α ≤ 2 is any fixed constant, whereas, the complexity of the same problems in transitive tournaments is O(n).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the selection problem is polynomial-time in the case of the transitive tournaments, it is NP-complete for the non-transitive tournaments.
the problem of recognizing certain directed trees in tournaments is as hard as finding certain directed trees in general tournaments, which is in contrast to the case of transitivity.
the complexity of selecting vertices in a tournament Tn is Θ(kn) if k is a fixed non-negative constant, but Ω(n2) otherwise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complexity of the problem depends on the number of vertices of maximum outdegree.
in tournaments with few transitive subtournaments, the complexity of finding various types of trees is significantly higher.
, in general tournaments, the complexity of selection depends on the structure of the tree to be found.
